claims.text: Conventional single-phase ZrB2 typically requires processing above 2300 °C for full densification.
Prior lower-temperature ZrB2 specimens processed below 1700 °C exhibit incomplete densification and residual porosity.
Prior lower-temperature ZrB2 specimens have inadequate oxidation and liquid-metal corrosion resistance.
SPS using rapid heating and high uniaxial pressure can fully densify single-phase ZrB2 below 1700 °C.
SPS promotes rapid particle bonding in ZrB2.
SPS inhibits grain growth and produces a refined ZrB2 microstructure.
SPS produces highly dense ZrB2 with minimal porosity and fewer microcracks.
Rapid heating and pressure enhance atomic diffusion and interparticle bonding at lower overall processing temperatures.
A fine-grained, low-porosity ZrB2 microstructure improves mechanical strength and structural integrity.
Reduced porosity, microcracking, and defect density limit pathways for oxygen ingress and oxidation.
Reduced porosity, microcracking, and defect density limit liquid-metal infiltration and corrosion.
Short SPS exposure minimizes grain coarsening.
Avoiding prolonged high-temperature exposure improves the stability of protective surface oxides during oxidation or liquid-metal exposure.
SPS-processed ZrB2 will have mechanical performance comparable to or better than ZrB2 conventionally sintered above 2300 °C.
SPS-processed ZrB2 will outperform conventionally processed lower-temperature ZrB2 in mechanical strength.
SPS-processed ZrB2 will exhibit slower oxidation weight gain and less oxide-scale spallation.
SPS-processed ZrB2 will exhibit reduced liquid-metal penetration and corrosion-related mass loss.
The proposed benefits apply to oxidation in air at 1200–1400 °C.
The proposed benefits apply during exposure to a representative molten plating metal or plating alloy.

contradictions.description: The intervention is repeatedly specified as operating below or sub-1700 °C, but the proposed processing range is 1650–1700 °C and therefore includes 1700 °C rather than remaining strictly below it.
